blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The number skills a data question needs: the four operations, scale and representative fractions, mean and range, percentages, ratios and indices, significant figures, scatter relationships, drawing graphs and choosing scales.

blocks.heading: The four operations
blocks.text: Data work is the four operations used as the data requires. Totals by addition: the district's population is its age groups added. Change by subtraction: the growth of the town is this census minus the last. Rates by division: the density is the people divided by the area. Scaling by multiplication: the real distance is the map measurement times the scale. The answer is rounded to suit the figures, because a mean of individual measurements reported to five figures claims a precision the data does not have.

blocks.heading: Scale and representative fractions
blocks.text: A representative fraction such as 1:50 000 means 1 unit on the map is 50 000 of the same units on the ground: 1 centimetre on the map is 50 000 centimetres, which is 500 metres, on the ground. The conversion is multiplication by the denominator and a change to sensible units, and the scale line printed on the map does the same job graphically, which is what the paper edge method uses. On a 1:25 000 sheet, 1 centimetre is 250 metres on the ground.

blocks.heading: Mean and range
blocks.text: The mean is the total of the values divided by how many there are. Five daily rainfalls of 0, 2, 10, 6 and 2 millimetres total 0 + 2 + 10 + 6 + 2 = 20 millimetres, so the mean is 20 / 5 = 4 millimetres. The range is written from the lowest value to the highest, 0 to 10 millimetres, or their difference, 10 - 0 = 10 millimetres, when a single figure is asked for. A range keeps both its ends, its sign and its decimal places: one value alone is not a range, and a minus sign or a decimal dropped loses the precision the question asked to keep.

blocks.heading: Percentages, ratios and decimals
blocks.text: A percentage is the part divided by the whole, multiplied by 100. A town of 40 000 people with 9 000 under 15 has 9 000 / 40 000 x 100 = 22.5 per cent children. A ratio compares parts of a total: 9 000 children and 31 000 others stand in the ratio 9:31. A decimal or fraction converts to a percentage the same way, multiply by 100, so 0.225 is 22.5 per cent. The three forms answer the same question in different clothes, and the data question names which it wants.

blocks.heading: Standard notation and significant figures
blocks.text: Standard notation writes large and small numbers as a figure between 1 and 10 times a power of ten: 8 000 000 000 people is 8 x 10 to the power 9. A negative index marks a fraction: 0.001 is 1 x 10 to the power minus 3. Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit, so 30 400 is 3 to two significant figures but 30 000 to three, and the answer carries the precision the data supports: rainfall gauge readings to the nearest millimetre are not reported to three significant figures as if they were exact.

blocks.heading: Scatter relationships
blocks.text: A scatter graph shows the relationship between two measures, one on each axis. A positive relationship: the points rise together, more of one goes with more of the other, distance from the CBD against house price. A negative relationship: one falls as the other rises, distance from the CBD against land value in most cities. No relationship: the points scatter without a slope, a cloud with no direction. Reading the slope is reading the sign of the relationship, and the points, not the line of best fit alone, are the evidence.

blocks.heading: Drawing graphs
blocks.text: Graphs are drawn to their type. Bars for categories, equal widths, gaps between. Lines for time series, points joined. Divided bars or pie charts for shares of a total. Scatter for relationships. Each point is plotted accurately and each plotted value checked against its scale, because one misread axis scrambles the whole series. The axes are labelled with what they show and the units they show it in.

blocks.heading: Choosing scales and axes
blocks.text: A good graph uses most of the axis length, starts each axis at a value that lets the data fill the grid, and uses simple intervals, 0, 10, 20, 30, that a reader can count in. An axis squashed into the bottom third of the grid wastes the paper and flattens the trend; an axis starting at 0 when the data runs 490 to 510 crams every point into one square. The scale serves the data, and the choice of it is marked as part of the drawing.

blocks.heading: Ruler and protractor
blocks.text: A ruler measures to the nearest millimetre along the line being measured, the zero of the scale set on one end of the line, the reading taken square-on, not at an angle. A protractor's centre sits exactly on the point of the angle, its zero line along one arm, and the reading is taken on the scale that runs clockwise from that zero, the outer scale from the lower arm, the inner from the upper. Bearings use the same discipline: centre on the starting point, zero line along grid north, degrees read clockwise.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: These are the number skills the Paper 4 enquiries of topic 5 need: means and ranges of field data, percentages of survey results, and graphs drawn and scaled for the results tables there.

blocks.heading: The four operations, worked
blocks.text: The four operations, worked on a farm budget. A farm holds 240 cattle and sells 85 in the year: 240 - 85 = 155 remain. It buys 30 breeding cows: 155 + 30 = 185. Each cow drinks about 45 litres a day, so the herd needs 185 x 45 = 8325 litres a day. Watered by tanker loads of 5000 litres, that is 8325 / 5000 = 1.67 loads, so two loads a day in practice. Addition totals, subtraction finds change, multiplication scales, division shares out, and the worked chain shows all four in one farm's morning. Paper 2 sets one-mark parts on exactly these moves, and the unit follows the question.

blocks.heading: Representative fractions, worked
blocks.text: A representative fraction, worked. A map carries the fraction 1:50 000, which says 1 unit on the map is 50 000 of the same units on the ground: 1 centimetre stands for 50 000 centimetres, which is 500 metres, which is 0.5 kilometres. A ridge 6.2 centimetres long on the sheet is 6.2 x 0.5 = 3.1 kilometres of high ground. A planner who must fit a 4-kilometre canal onto the same sheet needs 4 / 0.5 = 8 centimetres of paper and knows it fits. The fraction converts both ways, ground to paper and paper to ground, and the scale line printed on the sheet does the same job for a ruler laid along it.

blocks.heading: Mean and range, worked
blocks.text: Mean and range, worked on five daily rainfalls: 0, 4, 12, 6 and 8 millimetres. The total is 0 + 4 + 12 + 6 + 8 = 30 millimetres, so the mean is 30 / 5 = 6 millimetres a day. The range is written from the lowest to the highest, 0 to 12 millimetres, or given as a single figure, 12 - 0 = 12 millimetres. The range keeps both its ends and its unit: an answer of 12 without the millimetres, or 6 alone offered as the range, loses the mark, because the range is the spread and not a value in it. Paper 2 asks for one or the other by name, and the words mean and range are not interchangeable.

blocks.heading: The range dropped or trimmed
blocks.text: The recorded error is giving one value as the range, or dropping a minus sign or a decimal place the question asks to keep. The correct move: the range is written from the lowest value to the highest, or their difference when a single figure is asked for, and the precision and sign stay as the data gives them. The test: are both ends of the range there, and is the answer exactly as precise as the question demands?

blocks.heading: Percentages and ratios, worked
blocks.text: Percentages and ratios, worked on a town of 30 000 people whose workforce of 12 000 splits: 5400 in services, 4800 in industry, 1800 in farming. The service share is 5400 / 12000 x 100 = 45 per cent, the industry share 4800 / 12000 x 100 = 40 per cent, the farm share 1800 / 12000 x 100 = 15 per cent, and the three total 100 because they are shares of one workforce. As a ratio, services to industry to farming stands at 54:48:18, which simplifies by dividing through by 6 to 9:8:3. The percentage and the ratio are two dressings of one fact, and the question names which it wants, so the answer gives that form and shows the working that produced it.

blocks.heading: Standard notation, worked
blocks.text: Standard notation, worked. A country's population of 2 500 000 is written as 2.5 x 10 to the power 6, because the figures from the first non-zero digit are 2, 5, and the decimal point has moved six places. A river's dissolved load of 0.003 grams per litre is 3 x 10 to the power minus 3, a negative index marking a value below one, with the point moved three places the other way. The form is a figure between 1 and 10 times a power of ten, and the power counts the moves. Comparisons become easy once the form is standard: 2.5 x 10 to the power 6 against 9.8 x 10 to the power 5 is a country a little over two and a half times the other, read off the powers at a glance.

blocks.heading: Significant figures, worked
blocks.text: Significant figures, worked. A census count of 47 128 people, given to two significant figures, is 47 000, because the third figure, 1, is below 5 and the 7 stands; given to one, it is 50 000, because the second figure, 7, lifts the 4 to a 5. A mean rainfall of 23.48 millimetres, itself the average of readings taken to the nearest millimetre, is honestly given as 23.5 to one decimal place, and 23.48 claims a precision the gauge never had. The rule counts from the first non-zero digit and rounds by the figure after the cut, and the honest answer carries no more figures than the data supports.

blocks.heading: Scatter relationships, worked
blocks.text: A scatter graph, worked. Shop floor area is plotted against daily takings for ten shops, and the points run from the lower left to the upper right in a loose band: the bigger the floor, the bigger the takings, a positive relationship, because both rise together. A second graph plots the same shops' distance from the bus station against their takings, and the band runs the other way, upper left to lower right: the farther the shop, the smaller the takings, a negative relationship. The sign of the slope is the finding, and one point that sits far off the band is an outlier, worth naming and worth explaining if the resource allows, because an outlier is a shop with something else going on. Paper 2 gives a mark for naming the relationship and a mark for reading a value off the best-fit line.

blocks.heading: Drawing a graph, worked
blocks.text: Drawing a graph, worked through one dataset: four towns' annual visitors, 9000, 6400, 4300 and 7200. The type: categories compared, so a bar chart, one bar per town, equal widths, gaps between. The axes: towns named across the bottom, a vertical axis scaled 0 to 10 000 marked every 1000, which lets the four bars fill the grid. The drawing: each bar's height read against the scale, 9000 nine units up, and drawn with a ruler. The labels: what each axis shows and the units, visitors and towns. A bar drawn freehand, an axis with no units or a bar of the wrong width each lose the drawing mark, because a graph is a measurement displayed, and the display has rules.

blocks.heading: Scales and axes, worked
blocks.text: Scales and axes, worked. Data run from 420 to 490 millimetres of annual rainfall, and a learner scales the axis from zero: the whole dataset crowds into the top fifth of the grid, and the differences the study exists for vanish. The better axis starts at 400 and runs to 500, marked every 20, so the values spread across the paper and the variation shows. The axis that does not start at zero says so on its labels, because a reader who assumes zero is misled by the steepened slopes. The second rule is simple intervals: 0, 20, 40, 60, a reader can count in, not 0, 17, 34, 51, which nobody can. The scale serves the data, and the grid serves the scale.

blocks.heading: Ruler and protractor, worked
blocks.text: Ruler and protractor, worked. A distance on a map measures 7.4 centimetres: the ruler's zero is set on one end, not its worn edge, the eye squares over the 7.4 mark, and the reading is taken square and not at a slant. A bearing is measured with the protractor's centre dot exactly on the start point, its zero line along grid north, and the degrees read on the clockwise scale from that zero, which is the outer scale when north is up. A pie slice of 25 per cent is drawn as 25 / 100 x 360 = 90 degrees, a right angle, measured from the slice's starting radius. The instruments are simple, and their marks go to the learner who uses them exactly, centre on the point, zero on the line, eye square over the reading.

blocks.heading: The arithmetic of a field study, worked
blocks.text: The arithmetic a field study needs, worked on one river dataset. Five width readings, in metres: 2.4, 2.8, 3.1, 2.9, 3.3. The total is 2.4 + 2.8 + 3.1 + 2.9 + 3.3 = 14.5 metres, so the mean width is 14.5 / 5 = 2.9 metres. The range runs from 2.4 to 3.3 metres, a spread of 3.3 - 2.4 = 0.9 metres. A cross-section's area, roughly the mean width times the mean depth of 0.6 metres, is 2.9 x 0.6 = 1.74 square metres, and a float timed over 10 metres in 25 seconds gives a speed of 10 / 25 = 0.4 metres per second, so the discharge, the area times the speed, is 1.74 x 0.4 = 0.696, about 0.7 cubic metres per second. One dataset, and the whole of this unit's arithmetic appears in it, means, ranges, multiplications and divisions, each carrying its unit.

blocks.heading: A percentage chain, worked
blocks.text: A percentage chain, worked on a settlement's data. A village of 2400 people holds 1560 people of working age. The working share is 1560 / 2400 x 100 = 65 per cent, so the dependent share is 100 - 65 = 35 per cent, or 2400 - 1560 = 840 people. Of those 840, a survey finds 600 under 15 and 240 over 65, so the young dependants are 600 / 840 x 100 = 71 per cent of the dependent group, rounded from 71.4. As a ratio of young to elderly dependants, 600:240 simplifies by dividing through by 120 to 5:2. Every step is the same move, the part over the whole times 100, applied to whatever whole the question names, the village, the dependants, and the discipline is naming the whole before dividing by it, because the commonest slip is the right share of the wrong whole.

blocks.heading: Graphs drawn and read, worked
blocks.text: Graphs drawn and read, one last worked set. A divided bar: a country's energy from coal 45 per cent, hydro 35, solar 20, drawn on a 10-centimetre bar as 45 / 100 x 10 = 4.5 centimetres of coal, 3.5 of hydro and 2 of solar, each segment shaded to a stated key. A line graph: the river study's five width readings against distance downstream, 2.4, 2.8, 3.1, 2.9, 3.3 at sites one to five, plotted and joined, and the line shows the channel widening downstream with a dip at site four. Reading it back: the trend rises overall, from 2.4 metres to 3.3, with the site-four dip as the exception worth explaining, a boulder field slowing the flow perhaps. Drawing and reading are the two halves of one skill, and the reader reads what the drawer drew, which is why the drawing rules exist.

blocks.heading: How Paper 2 sets the arithmetic
blocks.text: How the paper sets the arithmetic. The syllabus lists these skills as part of Paper 2's techniques: the four operations, map scale and representative fractions, mean and range, averages, decimals, fractions, percentages and ratios, standard notation with positive and negative indices, significant figures, scatter relationships, drawing and interpreting the listed graphs, selecting scales and axes, and using a ruler and protractor. They are not set as pure sums: each arrives attached to a geographical resource, a population to total, a map to convert, a survey to average, so each number is the answer to a geography question, and that is also the best way to learn them, practising on data that means something, because a figure with a unit and a place is remembered where a bare figure is not.
